title: Communications Intelligence/Electromagnetic Warfare Operator
overview: Communications Intelligence (COMINT)/Electromagnetic Warfare (EW) Operators exploit every phase of communications signals and digital network systems by engaging in collection, processing, exploitation, dissemination, and analysis. Additional skills include planning, coordinating, and executing signals intelligence (SIGINT) and electromagnetic warfare (EW) operations from start to finish while utilizing both programs of record equipment as well as commercially acquired equipment. Operators must perform communications electronic signals search missions, record intercepts of signals using electronic means, and measure, classify, and evaluate signals. Operators must be familiar with communications intercept receivers, specialized computer hardware and software programs, and wideband converters used in the process of collecting, recording, analyzing, and reporting on a wide variety of intercepted communications signals. Operators will conduct and support full spectrum EW operations encompassing electromagnetic warfare support, electromagnetic attack, and the correct reporting thereof. Marines must be familiar with the conduct of SIGINT, EW, and cyber operations in support of the marine air ground task force (MAGTF) at both team and battalion levels and be prepared to contribute to each as deemed necessary by the unit commander.

ai.blurb: Finds, records and makes sense of enemy radio and network signals, and jams or disrupts them when ordered.
ai.dayToDay: Much of the work happens in a secure, windowless space or a cramped vehicle shelter, wearing headphones and watching waterfall displays for signals worth collecting. You'll search, intercept, classify and report traffic, then write it up for analysts and commanders — long stretches of patience punctuated by a short burst of something important. title: Signals Intelligence/Electromagnetic Warfare Technician
overview: This is a PMOS that requires signals intelligence (SIGINT), electromagnetic warfare (EW), and support to cyberspace operations (CO) training focused on collection management, operational planning and coordination, analysis, reporting, exploitation, and dissemination in support of the seven warfighting functions. Duties encompass the supervision of tasking, collection, processing, exploitation, and dissemination of products related to the three disciplines of SIGINT: communications intelligence (COMINT), electronic intelligence (ELINT), and foreign instrumentation signals intelligence (FISINT). EW duties encompass the planning, coordination, and execution of full spectrum MAGTF EW operations including electromagnetic warfare support (ES), electromagnetic protect (EP), and electromagnetic attack (EA). Provides intelligence support to full spectrum CO defined as offensive cyberspace operations (OCO), defensive cyberspace operations (DCO), and DOD information network operations (DODIN). Technicians develop and maintain records on technical aspects of target emitters, develop and maintain communications order of battle files, situation maps, and other related SIGINT/EW/CO files. Technicians prepare and issue reports to include intelligence reports, technical reports, and summaries. Technicians are required to perform SIGINT/EW/CO briefings. This MOS is career progression for MOSs 2621, 2631, and 2641. MOS 2629 is assigned upon promotion to SSgt. Marines who are assigned an EMOS of 2712 through 2796 shall take the Defense Language Proficiency Test (DLPT) annually and shall maintain a minimum proficiency of L2/R2 on the Defense Language Proficiency Test (DLPT) in their assigned 27XX language(s), in accordance with reference (bb). Preferred target for assignment to career progression training is at the 5-8 years’ time in service (TIS) mark.

title: Cryptologic Language Analyst
overview: Cryptologic Language Analysts (CLA) monitor, transcribe, and translate intercepted target foreign communications; exploit every phase of designated foreign communications by engaging in collection, processing, exploitation, analysis, and reporting; and install, operate, and perform preventive maintenance of program of record as well as commercially acquired intercept equipment. Duties encompass all facets of signals intelligence (SIGNT), electronic warfare (EW) and cyber operations in support of the MAGTF at both team and battalion levels and must be prepared to contribute to each as deemed necessary by the unit commander. Marines shall periodically (annually or biennially, dependent on scores) retake the defense language proficiency test (DLPT) and shall maintain a minimum proficiency of Listening 2/Reading (L2/R2) DLPT in their assigned 27XX language(s), in accordance with reference (bb). Formal intermediate and advanced language training is available and will be afforded to CLAs no later than upon PCS from their first duty station. Per DoDI 3300.07, CLAs will engage, during normal duty hours, a minimum of 160 hours of formal language training every 24 months. MOS 2629, SIGINT/EW/CO Technician, is assigned upon promotion to a staff sergeant. Marines shall maintain language proficiency in their assigned 27XX language(s) upon assignment of MOS 2629.

ai.blurb: Listens to intercepted foreign communications, transcribes and translates them, and turns what's said into intelligence reports.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens in a secure, windowless facility with headphones on, or in a shelter with a radio battalion team in the field. You'll spend hours listening to audio in Arabic, Chinese, Korean, Russian, Persian or another assigned language, transcribing, translating and writing up what matters, alongside analysts and equipment operators. You also set up and maintain your own intercept gear, and you're required to keep doing formal language training throughout your career — the language decays fast if you don't.
ai.funFact: Before you get near the job you'll likely spend a year or more at the Defense Language Institute in Monterey, California — one of the most intensive language schools anywhere, where the day is largely classroom immersion in your target language.

title: Intelligence Surveillance Reconnaissance (ISR) Systems Engineer
overview: ISR Systems Engineers design and implement the integration and management of ISR platforms, intelligence datasets, and intelligence networks as members of the signals intelligence and all-source intelligence production chains. These duties include but are not limited to sensor integration, ensuring dataflow between intelligence systems, Sensitive Compartmented Information communications, maintain data standardization, enterprise support and services, network and data redundancy, and disaster recovery. Marines assigned this MOS receive training in computer hardware fundamentals, operating systems, information assurance, database and data flow management, radio frequency theory, satellite communications, networking, system integration, network and data science philosophies. This MOS will be assigned and voided only by the authority of the CMC (MM). Marines in this MOS may be assigned to a BIC [within their occupational field] that has been coded with one or more DoD Cyber Workforce Framework (DCWF) work role codes. Please reference DoDI 8140.10, DoDM 8140.10, and the MOS roadmap for additional training and certification requirements associated with these work role codes.

title: Intelligence Data and Technology Chief
overview: The Intelligence Data and Technology Chief is an intelligence systems technologist that is responsible for the design and implementation of their organization operational architecture to address intelligence requirements. They integrate data science techniques, emerging technologies, and National Intelligence Community capabilities into their architecture. Marines are employed in the planning process and responsible for the development of an intelligence communications plan that integrates systems, software, personnel, and data within their organization. Intelligence Data and Technology Chiefs implement data security, intelligence community policy and guidelines, currently fielded operational equipment, available alternate technology, and emerging technology to interact with intelligence and non-intelligence data sources. Additional responsibilities include planning and deploying machine learning tools, neural networks, and artificial intelligence capabilities within their organization architecture. Marines are assigned as data architects and function as senior advisors to the Chief Technology Officer Headquarters Marine Corps, the staff at the MEF and COCOM level, and in all levels of the marine air-ground task force (MAGTF).

SIGINT/EW Chiefs also supervise the activities of personnel performing communications intercept, electronic reconnaissance, radio direction finding, analysis and reporting functions, intelligence support to CO, and EW operations. They may also be assigned to the intelligence staff marine corps forces special operations command (MARSOC), marine cryptologic support battalion (MCSB), radio battalions, marine littoral regiments (MLR), and the staff sections of the MEF information groups (MIG), marine divisions (MARDIV), marine corps forces commands, and marine aviation wings (MAW) supervising special security and special intelligence support functions. Additionally, they serve in staff billets as operational advisors designated by the commander or cognizant staff officer.

title: Digital Wideband Systems Maintainer
overview: Digital Wideband Systems Maintainers are trained to install, diagnose, modify, and perform field level maintenance on digital wideband communications equipment used for high capacity, troposcatter and satellite link communications. Typical duties include tuning and aligning systems, adjusting audio or data levels, using test equipment to make checks on circuit quality, diagnose equipment faults to the component level, and replacing faulty parts or components at an organizational or intermediate maintenance activity. These Marines submit field service maintenance requests to conduct technical research, order parts, repair, restore and assist in the installation of Digital Wideband Systems. Journeyman level Maintainers, with a minimum of three years of experience, reconcile repair parts and records of systems within the active and maintenance closeout phases, make recommendations pertaining to maintenance resource allocations and guide in the installation of digital wideband systems. Additionally, these Marines provide quality control inspections of maintenance tasks. These Marines guide novice Marines through non-routine maintenance tasks and develop competencies of those Marines. Marines in this MOS may be assigned to a BIC (within their occupational field) that has been coded with one or more DoD cyber workforce framework (DCWF) work role codes. Please reference DoDI 8140.10, DoDM 8140.10, and the MOS roadmap for additional training and certification requirements associated with these work role codes.

overview: Calibration Technicians are qualified to perform calibration of mechanical, length, mass, and low complexity electronic Test Measurement and Diagnostic Equipment (TMDE) utilized within the Marine Corps. Typical duties include the calibration and repair of mechanical, length, mass, and low complexity TMDE while adhering to the associated maintenance processes and metrology documentation established within the appropriate references. Journeyman Calibration Technicians are trained to perform the calibration of increasingly complex TMDE and maintenance support equipment. Typical duties include the calibration, troubleshooting, repair, modification, and adjustment of increasingly complex TMDE, advanced level troubleshooting, and repairs of enterprise support equipment. These technicians may also supervise ground maintenance activities which include the execution of maintenance, maintenance administration, MOS skill training, supporting quality control programs, processing shipments of delicate TMDE to/from depot support, and assisting with the deployment/employment of the calibration facility. These technicians assist with the associated maintenance management and metrology requirements outside of a routine nature. Marines in this MOS may be assigned to a BIC (within their occupational field) that has been coded with one or more DoD cyber workforce framework (DCWF) work role codes. Please reference DoDI 8140.10, DoDM 8140.10, and the MOS roadmap for additional training and certification requirements associated with these work role codes.

ai.blurb: Checks and corrects the Marine Corps' test and measuring equipment so the readings everyone else relies on are actually true.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens indoors in a calibration lab, a temperature- and humidity-controlled room full of reference standards, torque wrenches, multimeters, gauges and scales. You compare a piece of equipment against a known standard, document everything to the letter, and repair or adjust it when it drifts out of tolerance. The pace is methodical rather than frantic, you work in a small shop of technicians, and paperwork is genuinely part of the job — a calibration nobody recorded properly didn't happen.
ai.funFact: The field is called metrology — the science of measurement — and it runs on a chain of traceability that ends at national standards held by NIST, so a torque wrench checked in a Marine lab is ultimately tied to the same references as the rest of the country.
goodFitIf: like precision over speed
enjoy fiddly hands-on troubleshooting
don't mind detailed paperwork
did well in algebra

title: Ground Supply Officer (I)
overview: Ground Supply Officers are a special staff officer that supervise the commanders' property, plant, & equipment (PP&E) and operating material & supplies (OM&S) to ensure data accuracy, existence, and completeness (equipment accountability, visibility, and auditability). They supervise and coordinate ground supply administration and operations for supply activities, units, bases, or stations, to include operating forces and shore station organizations. Ground Supply Officers may direct the activities of a maintenance distribution or industrial type organization. They command or serve in either an operating forces service unit or a non- operating forces activity. Ground Supply Officers supervise the execution of supply chain management policies and procedures pertaining to procurement, receipt, inventory control, repair, storage, distribution, issue, disposal, and computation and maintenance of stock positioning requirements. They provide supply support insight for operational planning requirements, supervise transportation of supplies and equipment, manage the transmittal of public funds, participate in the budget process, administer and expend allotted funds, and make necessary recommendations to the commanding officer regarding supply support procedures.

title: Ground Supply Chain Management Officer (III)
overview: Ground Supply Operations Officers are technical experts who are trained and appointed in writing to supervise and coordinate the technical activities of a supply section of the operating forces or a shore station organization. They may command or serve as a special staff officer. They advise the commander on supply related matters and provide recommended courses of action. They supervise and coordinate the technical aspects of retail (using unit and intermediate) and wholesale-level supply activities in the operating forces, supporting establishments, and with other supporting agencies. They provide the technical knowledge of automated supply systems necessary to ensure timely and accurate processing of supply related ADP systems. They provide liaison between supply sections and supporting data processing activities. They supervise supply chain management to include procurement; receipt; inventory control (i.e. forecasting/stock determination); storage; distribution; issue; disposal; and computation and maintenance of stock positioning requirements. They supervise the maintenance of subsistence, clothing, ammunition, and inventory control accounts. Ground Supply Operations Officers assist in the budget execution; fund justification; administration and expenditure of allotted funds; and make recommendations to the commanding officer regarding supply support issues. They provide supply support insight for operational planning requirements; supervise transportation of supplies and equipment; manage the transmittal of public funds; participate in the budget process, administer, and expend allotted funds; and make necessary recommendations to the commanding officer regarding supply support procedures.

title: Operational Contract Support (OCS) Specialist
overview: PMOS 3044 is a lateral move into the OCS career field. The PMOS integrates highly qualified enlisted Marines into the acquisition field whose mission is to deploy in support of the full range of military operations, as directed under the department of defense (DoD). Marines serving in this PMOS will be designated members of the Defense Acquisition Workforce and Contingency Contracting Force (CCF), which is governed under references (co) and (cp). Marines in this PMOS are equipped with the contracting fundamentals required to procure supplies and services for operations, exercises, contingencies, natural disasters, foreign training events, garrison environments, and advise senior leaders in business solutions and concepts. Supplies and services will be procured in accordance with governing regulations. Marines in this PMOS must have the ability to communicate effectively in order to interact with other branches of the DoD, civilian and military workforce, the commercial sector, host nations and their workforce. Marines in this PMOS may participate in formal apprenticeship programs leading to a Department of Labor Certificate of Apprenticeship; refer to reference (bs) for specific information concerning the united services military apprenticeship program. Overall, Marines are required to operate independently, self-manage workloads, apply sound business management principles, fulfill acquisition workforce continuous learning requirements, and pursue higher education. Marines desiring lateral move into the 3044 MOS must submit a lateral move request in accordance with MCO 4200.34.
requirements: Must be screened and approved by a 3044 MOS screening board.
Must possess a GT score of 105 or higher on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery Test.
Must demonstrate excellent written and oral communication skills by completing an essay with a minimum of 500 words.
Waivers to any prerequisite or requirements must be submitted to and approved by the 3044 occupational field manager.
Must be a tier 1 or 2 category reported from the reenlistment extension lateral move (RELM) request, commanding officer's tier evaluation.
Corporals from any PMOS must have a minimum of 36-months-time-in- service. Sergeants from any PMOS must have no more than 12-months-time-in- grade.
Security requirement: Must have a final adjudicated secret security clearance based on national agency check, law enforcement and credit check (NACLC).
Must be worldwide deployable at the time Marine is approved for lateral move into the 3044 PMOS and meet criteria for reenlistment set forth in reference (bj).
Must submit letters of recommendation from their current officer- in-charge and staff noncommissioned officer in charge to the 3044 MOS screening board.

Must have a minimum of 36 months of obligated service upon completion of on-the-job training (OJT) and assignment of PMOS 3044. Marines must request an extension of obligated service in order to comply with reference (bj).

Must not have any felony convictions by a court-martial or civilian court. Marines must also not have any non-judicial punishments (NJP) in current grade and have never received NJP for dereliction in the performance of duties, larceny, theft, and fraud, misappropriation of government funds or property, or financial irresponsibility.

Must be interviewed by a Marine Corps field contracting system (MCFCS) office or Marine Forces Special Operations Command (MARSOC) contracting office and receive endorsement from the procurement chief or chief of contracting office recommending approval or disapproval of lateral move. For unique circumstances, telephonic or virtual interviews are permitted.

Upon approval for lateral move into the PMOS 3044, Marines are initially assigned the intended military occupational specialty (IMOS) 3000. After completion of 24 months OJT, training requirements governed by reference (co), and Defense Acquisition Workforce Improvement Act (DAWIA) Contracting Professional certification, Marines shall be assigned PMOS 3044. PMOS 3044 assignment requires an official letter from the Marine with an endorsement from the chief of contracting (see MCO 4200.34) sent to the local Installation Personnel Administration Center. PMOS 3044 Marines fill professional acquisition billets governed by reference (co), which outlines the required fundamental training standards for personnel serving in government acquisition billets. The Defense Acquisition University (DAU) is the agency mandated by DAWIA to provide the required professional education to all government agencies. (a) Continued skills progression and career enhancement courses are listed in the PMOS road map. (b) Reference (co) declares that Defense Acquisition Workforce members must acquire 80 continuous learning points (CLPs) every two years from the date of entry into the acquisition workforce for as long as the member remains in an acquisition position.

Failure to maintain or complete requirements for continued qualification and progression may result in removal from the PMOS for the following reasons: (a) Admission of guilt or issuance of a guilty verdict as a result from a criminal prosecution or ethics violation. (b) Failure to meet the minimal performance standards, technical proficiency, DAWIA certification, and competency of the CCF PMOS. (c) Permanent loss of security clearance for any reason will result in removal or separation from PMOS per current MMEA guidelines and applicable MCOs. (d) Determined unsuitable for the CCF by the chief of contracting office, with an endorsement from the 3044 occupational field manager. A determination of unsuitability for the PMOS will not be held as a punitive action in the Marines record.

title: Supply Chain Manager
overview: Supply Chain Manager are responsible for executing, tracking, and managing the end-to-end flow of goods and services from the requestor to the receiver across both tactical and non-tactical operations. Their responsibilities span a wide range of functions including customer service, life cycle management, warehousing, financial management, inventory control, property accountability, storage operations, and secondary reparable management. These Marines are proficient in Department of Defense and Service-unique supply chain programs and possess a working knowledge of DoD financial systems to effectively budget and track funds from obligation through liquidation. They play a critical role in enabling both strategic and tactical objectives including distributed and expeditionary operations by leveraging supply chain capabilities in both contested and uncontested environments to ensure continuous and responsive logistical support. A key component of their role is managing high-value equipment across its entire lifecycle while mitigating significant follow-on costs. This requires cost- conscious planning, strategic sustainment decisions, and continuous optimization of supply chain performance. Supply Chain Managers understand that total ownership costs extend beyond procurement to include training, maintenance, upgrades, and disposal. Programs such as the Service Life Extension Program (SLEP) help maximize asset value and defer expensive replacements, delivering long-term cost savings. To reduce operational waste and improve responsiveness, these Marines employ supply chain optimization strategies leveraging tools like ERP systems, real-time data, Just-In-Time inventory, and vendor-managed inventory to enhance forecasting, agility, and resource efficiency. Careful budget planning and responsible fund allocation ensure that mission-critical requirements are met while maintaining fiscal discipline and accountability. Supply Chain Managers advise and assist the Supply Officer on all supply matters, giving commanders flexibility to align skilled personnel with priority missions and high-density projects. Through collaboration with other services, industry partners, and civilian logistics experts, these Marines drive cost-effective solutions and innovation while reinforcing readiness. In essence, the Marine Corps Supply Chain's approach to logistics emphasizes agility, resilience, and technological innovation grounded in fiscal responsibility to ensure sustained readiness and the smart use of every taxpayer dollar. This MOS serves as a career progression path for corporals holding MOSs 3043 and 3051.

title: Inventory Management Specialist
overview: Inventory Management Specialists perform a wide range of logistics and warehousing functions across the supply chain, including receiving, inspecting, locating, storing, rotating (first-in, first-out), safeguarding, issuing, preparing, shipping, returning, and disposing of materiel and equipment. They maintain automated or manual locator systems to conduct inventories, track issued durable goods and monitor shelf-life items. They also manage hazardous materials in accordance with classification and Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS). These Marines perform data entry transactions, retrieve historical records, and utilize handheld optical character recognition (OCR) scanners, multimedia retrieval systems, and other logistics technologies. They are licensed to operate Material Handling Equipment (MHE) in both garrison and deployed environments, including bulk and small parts conveyor systems used in automated warehousing operations. Marines in this MOS receive, sort, document, and store inventory, and prepare, pack, and issue items in open, enclosed, or hazardous material storage areas. They apply technical data to develop and execute care and storage plans, including calculating storage space requirements by weight, cube, and clearance factors across various supply categories.

title: Distribution Management Officer (II/III) (LtCol to Capt) and
overview: Distribution Management Officers (DMOs) are technical experts who are trained, certified, and appointed in writing to provide efficient, responsive, and quality transportation services within the assigned area of responsibility and ensure compliance with governing laws, directives, systems or programs, and regulations for cargo, passenger, personal property, and unit moves. They provide technical direction, management, and evaluation of the traffic management and unit movement aspects of the Department of Defense (DoD) transportation movement program on a worldwide basis, subject to the overall guidance, policies, and programs established by United States Transportation Command (USTRANSCOM), the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), and DoD Components. DMOs serve throughout the MAGTF, Headquarters Marine Corps, joint organizations, COCOMs, and supporting establishments. They are responsible for multiple procurement actions, financial documentation, and payment processes for transportation services as governed within authorized policies and applicable U.S. government contracting laws. DMOs make management decisions facilitating the execution of transportation entitlements for military members, dependents, and civilian employees; and act as the contracting officer representative (COR) for various transportation service provider contracts. They provide technical knowledge of automated information systems which deliver in-transit visibility of DoD unit and non-unit cargo, passengers, and personal property. As subject matter experts, they advise the commander on distribution and transportation related matters, provide recommended courses of action, and articulate current and future strategic distribution management requirements to the appropriate agencies. This MOS is technical in nature and requires years of training, education, and experience to become proficient.

title: Distribution Specialist
overview: Distribution Specialists are educated, equipped, and trained to manage fleet marine force requirements at the tactical, operational, strategic, and enterprise level. The specialists use federal, DoD, and service regulations, the defense transportation system (DTS), commercial modes of transportation, and distribution logistic functions to enable optimal selection and procurement of commercial and government- operated land, air, and sea transportation services. They use a variety of automated systems in the performance of their duties. Warehousing, rail, motor and air terminal operations, materiel handling, packing, packaging, preservation, and marking are daily operations. Distribution Specialists perform technical distribution management duties pertaining to movement of civilian and military personnel and their eligible family members both individually and in groups, using all modes of transportation. This includes planning for troop movements via chartered air, train, or bus, as well as port calls for overseas permanent change of station. The specialists perform personal property counseling interviews to advise members and eligible family members of their personal property shipping entitlements. The specialists perform additional operational duties and tasks at military and commercial air terminals. The specialists perform passport and visa services by counseling members and dependents on required documents, foreign clearance regulations, and by aiding in the preparation and submission of required correspondence to the Department of State and foreign embassies. This includes preparing all freight shipment documents to manifest cargo and passengers aboard government or commercial chartered conveyances. At the operational level, specialists perform in-theater sustainment, receiving, shipping, in-transit visibility, and distribution functions.

title: Food Service Officer (II/III) (LtCol to Capt) and
overview: Food Service Officers are special staff officers that supervise and manage the commanders' food service and subsistence program. They act as an interface between the commander and a wide variety of logistics agencies and organizations, while working closely with finance and supply communities to ensure the proper execution and expenditure of MPMC 1105 appropriated funds. Food Service Officers serve as technical advisers to commanders at all levels within the MAGTF, as well as supporting organizations, on the appropriate employment of food service personnel and equipment capabilities. They lead, coordinate, and integrate tailoring actions in support of the Maritime Prepositioning Force (MPF) Program, as well as the Marine Corps Prepositioning Program-Norway (MCPP-N). Food Service Officers ensure that combat feeding platforms are tailored and aligned with maritime expeditionary warfare capabilities throughout the prepositioning network. Food Service Officers plan, direct, coordinate, integrate, execute and/or supervise the execution of operations, and sustain operational forces throughout the conflict continuum for all operations, humanitarian assistance, crisis response activities, contingencies, and exercises. Food Service Officers analyze, translate, and execute commanders’ intent and operational requirements to support mission requirements across the enterprise. When forward deployed and during combat operations, or in support of humanitarian assistance/disaster relief, civil-military operations, distributed maritime operations, or other remote environments where DoD approved food sources are not established, Food Service Officers plan, direct, and coordinate actions with DoD agencies and appropriate medical authorities to ensure safe and hazardous-free food sources are obtained. When assigned to an installation command, Food Service Officers coordinate and manage installation messing and food service support, as well as perform quality control inspections of mess hall operations. They coordinate food service and mess activities at installations, units, bases, and stations, to include operating forces and shore station organizations. They provide technical assistance with planning, budgeting, procurement, and functional layout of mess hall equipment and furniture. They shape and influence the design of dining facility construction, and rehabilitation projects for food service facilities. They administer the menu development and nutrition awareness program. This MOS is technical in nature and requires years of experience to become proficient. Due to the diversity of commands throughout the Marine Corps, some of the duties and tasks performed by the Food Service Officer may overlap with those of the supply officer and/ or logistics officer. Additional billet roles may include assignment as company commander, formal school faculty, acquisition and cross-servicing arrangements (ACSA) manager, requirements development technician in coordination with the Capabilities Integration Officer at CD&I, OccFld specialist, and operations officer.

title: Food Service Specialist
overview: Food Service Specialists function in the garrison and field environments in every aspect of food preparation and cooking, program management and administration, procurement, storage, and distribution of subsistence supplies; requisitioning, purchasing, receiving, accountability, rotating (first in-first-out), and safekeeping of subsistence supplies, meal activity and consumption reporting. Additionally, they perform various duties within the Class I logistics chain management to include receiving, inspecting, locating, storing, issuing, preparing, shipping, material return, and disposal of materiel and equipment. Food Service Specialists maintain and operate automated information technology systems in order to maintain accountability of all subsistence inventories, input data entry transactions and retrieval of historical records; maintain records of perishable and non- perishable subsistence supplies, maintain record of Class I subsistence issued, and monitor shelf-life items. In support of the maritime prepositioning force (MPF) program and the marine corps prepositioning program-Norway (MCPP-N), they ensure that combat feeding platforms (e.g., combat rations and field feeding equipment) are tailored and aligned with maritime expeditionary warfare capabilities through the prepositioning network. When assigned to an installation food service program office, they perform quality assurance surveillance of food service contracts. The most senior grades act as senior enlisted advisors and administrative assistants to the food service officer/food service operations officer. These specially trained technicians are also responsible for the design and functional layout of expeditionary field feeding sites employed for military operations and humanitarian aid. Marines of the 3381 occupational specialties also provide expeditionary Class I feeding support for marine expeditionary units (MEUs) and airfields.

title: Finance Officer (III)
overview: Finance Officers serve as agents of the U.S. Treasury and are responsible and pecuniary liable for the disbursement, collection, accounting, and safeguarding of all public funds entrusted to them. They are responsible for the proper execution and adherence to policies and procedures governing the valid and legal disbursement/collection of public funds. They are responsible for the maintenance of the payments generated from the master military pay account (MMPA), the computation and payment of travel entitlements, as well as other miscellaneous payments paid to or on behalf of military personnel or the Marine Corps. They are as fiscal agents responsible for the timely and accurate reporting of all expenditures and collections into the accounting system. They are advisors to the local commanders and staff, in both a garrison and deployed environment, on all matters concerning the technical aspects of military pay and allowances, the disbursement/collection of official funds, and the laws, regulations, and directives governing their duties and other activities of the command. In garrison, they supervise and direct the operation of the finance office and are responsible for its performance. When deployed, Finance Officers supervise and direct disbursing detachments in support of the deployed commander and the Disbursing Officer. They interpret regulations and directives formulating policies and procedures related to military pay, travel, and fiscal matters within the office and for deployed detachments. They are responsible for the formulation and adherence to adequate internal controls to govern the operations of finance offices and disbursing detachments. The appropriate command shall initiate MOS reclassification for any Marine in this MOS who receives NJP or is convicted by court-martial or civilian court for any offense involving larceny, theft, fraud, falsifying financial records, misuse of the government travel charge card (GTCC), or misuse of public funds. This MOS will be voided only by the authority of CMC.

title: Judge Advocate (I)
overview: Judge Advocates provide legal support to commanders, Marines, Sailors, and their families to promote readiness and to contribute to mission accomplishment. Judge advocates provide legal support in the following six functions: military justice, international and operational law, administrative law, civil law, legal assistance, and legal administration. As company grade officers, judge advocates ordinarily serve at law centers as litigators or legal assistance attorneys, or in staff judge advocate offices as command legal advisors. Litigation opportunities exist as special trial, trial, defense, and victims legal counsel in courts- martial; as Special Assistant United States Attorneys in United States Federal Court; and as recorders, counsel for the respondent, or victims’ legal counsel in administrative discharge boards. As majors, Judge Advocates may serve as staff judge advocates or deputy staff judge advocates providing command legal advice, or as litigators in the billets of special trial counsel, military justice officer, senior defense counsel, or regional victims legal counsel. Lieutenant Colonels may serve as staff judge advocates, deputy staff judge advocates, regional special trial counsel, regional trial counsel, regional defense counsel, or Law Center Directors. ai.blurb: A lawyer in uniform: prosecutes and defends courts-martial, advises commanders, and helps Marines with personal legal problems.
ai.dayToDay: Most junior judge advocates work out of a law center or a staff judge advocate's office on a base, doing the sort of things lawyers do anywhere — reading files, interviewing witnesses, drafting advice, appearing in court. One week you might be trying a court-martial, the next explaining a will or a landlord dispute to a lance corporal, or telling a colonel why his plan needs rethinking. The clients are Marines, Sailors and their families, and the law runs from military justice to the rules governing operations overseas.
ai.funFact: Some Marine judge advocates serve as Special Assistant United States Attorneys, prosecuting cases in federal court alongside civilian prosecutors; later in a career, field grade officers screened by a board can sit as military judges.

You can argue without losing your temper
You like writing and careful reading
You want courtroom time early

title: Legal Services Specialist
overview: The Legal Services Specialist MOS encompasses every facet of legal administration and management. General duties involve the provision of administrative support, research and investigation support, client relations support, and technical and logistical support incident to a law center or staff judge advocate office. Typical duties include research, preparation, and typing of general correspondence, forms, reports, wills, powers of attorney, and other documents dealing with legal and quasi-legal matters; checking all completed work for typographic accuracy; maintaining office files; interacting with clients; managing facilities and supplies; and, if senior in grade, acting as the legal services chief and senior enlisted advisor to the senior judge advocate in the office, with responsibility for the overall assignment, performance, training, counseling, morale, discipline, and welfare of all enlisted personnel. Selected Marines may attend follow-on training at the Legal Services Court Reporter Course to earn the NMOS 4422, Legal Services Court Reporter.

title: Communication Strategy and Operations Officer (I)
overview: The Communication Strategy and Operations (COMMSTRAT) officer holds the primary responsibility for communication engagement with all internal and external publics and audiences on behalf of the commander and for the execution of all plans and activities within the functions of Combat Camera (COMCAM) and Public Affairs (PA). The COMMSTRAT officer is the principal advisor to commanders and staff on communication and visual information matters at all levels and supports all operational planning. Typical duties include, but are not limited to developing and synchronizing communication plans; monitoring and assessing the communication aspects of the information environment, to include misinformation/disinformation identifying audiences, publics and stakeholders; identifying communication issues, risks and opportunities that may affect operations or institutional/ command reputation; conducting crisis communication; leading COMCAM and PA missions; developing annexes and appendices to operation plans; engaging with internal, domestic and international publics via traditional news media, social and/or emerging media, and face-to-face communication, to include community and key leader engagement; supervising review and release procedures; directing the development of written and visual information products; conducting communication training to assigned and supporting forces, to include media literacy and social media best practices; and providing support to recruiting operations.

title: Visual Information Officer (III)
overview: The Visual Information Officer (VIO) is a highly skilled technical expert in the 45XX occupational field, specializing in the application of organic visual information capabilities. Serving as the principal advisor to commanders and Communication Strategy and Operations (COMMSTRAT) Officers, the VIO provides expertise on all visual information matters. Their responsibilities include enhancing the proficiency and effectiveness of personnel by mentoring and training officers and Marines in mechanical, doctrinal, and conceptual aspects of visual information and serving as the Command Printing Officer. VIOs play a critical role in developing training, exercises, and operational plans that support mission- essential tasks, meet communication objectives, and ensure compliance with individual and collective training and readiness standards. They manage visual information equipment and commodities within their unit, ensuring operational readiness, and they regularly report on the unit's technical proficiency. VIOs have a comprehensive understanding of DOTMLPF-C (Doctrine, Organization, Training, Materiel, Leadership and Education, Personnel, Facilities, and Cost) from a program management perspective. They are responsible for requirements management, including forecasting and analyzing financial data to support informed decisions. Additionally, VIOs oversee indoctrination and certification programs, develop annexes and appendices to operational orders, integrate emerging technologies, review training and readiness manuals, and participate in advisory groups and trade shows. They may also serve as Combat Camera (COMCAM) planners, tasked with planning, sustaining, and employing COMCAM capabilities across various operational environments. In this capacity, they work closely with numbered fleets, Joint Force Commands (JFCs), and Headquarters Marine Corps (HQMC) to ensure the readiness of personnel and the successful execution of COMCAM operations.

title: Production Manager
overview: Production Managers serve as the principal sound engineer of a Marine Corps Fleet Band. Production Managers are responsible for additional duties in the bands marketing and communication section to support directed community relations plans, increase public awareness of the Marine Corps, and generate publicity for band performances. Additional internal duties include maintaining band press packages and managing the band official digital media platforms. They coordinate with communication strategy and operations offices for messaging guidance, cross-training opportunities, and support where larger production teams may be necessary. Production Managers must maintain a working knowledge of applicable copyright regulations, directives, and respective digital media user policies.

ai.blurb: Runs sound, lighting and media production for a Marine Corps band, plus its publicity and social media.
ai.dayToDay: You're the sound engineer behind a Fleet Band: setting up and mixing audio reinforcement, rigging stage and studio lighting, recording sessions and editing the results. A lot of the day is load-in, soundcheck, performance, load-out — often outdoors, often on the road — and the rest is planning gear purchases, advising the bandleader, and keeping the band's press materials and official social accounts current. You work closely with the musicians, band leadership and communication strategy staff, and you're expected to know copyright and media policy well enough to keep the band out of trouble.
ai.funFact: It isn't an entry-level job: you must already hold MOS 5524 and be picked by a technical evaluation board, with a recommendation from a bandleader and a serving production manager.
goodFitIf: You like live sound and lighting
You're calm during setup and teardown
You enjoy editing audio and video
You can manage gear and budgets

title: Instrument Repair Technician
overview: Instrument Repair Technicians are responsible for inspecting, maintaining, repairing, and overhauling all musical equipment assigned to a band, and they lead, train, and manage equipment support for band operations. Duties include organizing and maintaining the instrument repair shop according to current occupational safety and health standards; maintaining administrative records and repairs of work performed on musical instruments; and performing preventative maintenance on instrument repair tools and equipment. They perform various duties pertaining to the acquisition and inventory of band equipment and accessories and assist and advise the band officer on budgeting and purchase plans. As such, Instrument Repair Technicians must be knowledgeable and objective in applying purchasing and contracting laws and regulations. Marines in this MOS must have the ability to work independently.
requirements: Must possess MOS 5524.

Must be selected for PMOS 5523 through the 5523 PMOS technical evaluation board. Requests for PMOS 5523 must be accompanied by a technical evaluation and recommendation from a band officer or enlisted bandleader, and an instrument repair technician.
Must continue to make sufficient progress in MOS proficiency.
Must complete the Band Instrument Repair Course (C315591), Winona, MN.
training: Must complete the Band Instrument Repair Course (C315591), Winona, MN.

ai.blurb: Keeps a Marine band's instruments playable — repairing, overhauling and managing all the horns, drums and gear.
ai.dayToDay: Most of your work happens in a repair shop you run yourself: dent removal, pad replacement, valve and slide work, soldering, and the slow overhaul of instruments that have been hauled around the world. You also keep the paperwork straight — repair records, inventories, tool maintenance — and advise the band officer on what to buy and how to spend the budget within purchasing rules. It's quiet, independent work on a bench, punctuated by a trumpet player turning up with a problem an hour before a performance.
ai.funFact: The formal training is the Band Instrument Repair Course in Winona, Minnesota — a town long associated with instrument repair education in the United States.
goodFitIf: You like fixing delicate mechanical things
You already play in a band
You can work alone without supervision
You don't mind paperwork and budgets

title: Musician
overview: Musicians perform in a Marine Corps Band for concerts, parades, ceremonies, and various other official functions in support of the Marine Corps Bands’ mission. Musicians perform additional duties in support of band operations, such as unit supply, unit administrative assistant, and music librarian. Musicians are required to perform preventative maintenance on assigned musical equipment. Additional increased responsibilities relating to music performance are assigned based on grade/experience, such as instrument section leader or leader of a small ensemble. Musicians may be assigned to complete the Live Production Technician Course and be assigned additional duties of sound engineer.

MOS 5524 is assigned upon completing the Basic Music Course (N0355A2) at the Naval School of Music.

ai.dayToDay: Most of your time is rehearsal and performance — concerts, parades, change-of-command ceremonies and other official functions — plus the unglamorous half of band life: cleaning and maintaining instruments, running the music library, supply and admin paperwork. title: Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) Defense Officer (III)
overview: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, And Nuclear Defense (CBRND) Officers are technical advisers for operational and tactical functions associated with CBRN protection, CBRN response, and CBRN support to countering weapons of mass destruction (CWMD). They support an organization’s planning process by providing CBRN subject matter expertise for plans, annexes, orders, and standard operating procedures. CBRND Officers serving in protection billets develop plans to support their commander’s schemes of maneuver under CBRN conditions. CBRND Officers serving in response billets plan and lead CBRND support to the MAGTF and joint forces. CBRND Officers serving in CBRN analysis billets apply subject matter expertise to information and intelligence to develop a threat picture to guide the commanders planning and decision-making cycles. CBRND Officers in senior-level management billets (MEU, MEF, MARFOR) develop plans and advise commanders and staff on requirements related to activates and requirements to support combatant commander’s CWMD lines of effort and objectives within the supported area of operations. Marines entering this OccFld will initially receive a basic MOS 5701, Basic Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Defense Officer. Depending on the level of command, CBRND Officers will fill billets as CBRND/CWMD Plans Officer, CBRND Officers, CBRN Protection Officers, or CBRN Response Officers.
requirements: Must meet eligibility and appointment criteria as prescribed in MCO 1040.42, warrant officer (WO) and limited duty officer (LDO) accession programs.

Any 5701 officer who has not completed the CBRN Basic Warrant Officer Course after two years will be considered unqualified and subject to termination.

ai.blurb: Warrant officer who advises Marine commanders on fighting, surviving and planning in chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear conditions.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work is staff work: writing plans, annexes and standing operating procedures, briefing commanders, and sorting out what a unit needs to keep operating if a chemical or nuclear threat appears. Depending on the billet you might run detection and decontamination response teams, or sit on the analysis side turning intelligence into a threat picture. Expect command posts, planning cells and exercises as much as field kit, with periods in protective suits to prove it all works.
ai.funFact: This is a warrant officer track — you can't enlist straight into it; you have to be a sergeant or above first, then pass both Warrant Officer Basic Course at Quantico and the CBRN school at Fort Leonard Wood.

title: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) Defense Specialist
overview: CBRN Defense Specialists operate within the unit combat operations center to assist the staff in monitoring unit operations, facilitating warning and reporting, and coordinating CBRN response activities. CBRN Defense Specialists train personnel to employ individual and organizational CBRN equipment and execute individual survival measures to enable protective actions and sustain operations in a CBRN environment. CBRN Defense Specialists collect, analyze and provide information relative to CBR exposure status, location of contaminated areas and CBRN defense. Additionally, CBRN Defense Specialists maintain and prepare CBRN defense equipment for embarkation, deployment, and employment. This MOS is assigned and voided only by the authority of the CMC (MM).
requirements: Must be a U.S. citizen.
Must possess a GT score of 110 or higher.

ai.blurb: Prepares Marines to survive and keep fighting through chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear hazards, and tracks contamination when it happens.
ai.dayToDay: Much of the work happens in a unit's combat operations centre, watching reports, plotting where contamination is and advising the staff on what it means. The rest is hands-on and instructional: inspecting and maintaining masks, suits and detection gear, prepping it for embarkation, and running training so everyone in the unit knows how to use it. You'll spend a lot of time teaching people who'd rather be doing something else, which is part of the job.
ai.funFact: CBRN Marines train at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, home of the joint CBRN school — the same post where the Army's Chemical Corps, founded in WWI, does its training.

title: Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) Defense Chief
overview: The CBRN Defense Chief serves as a CBRN defense SME to advise the staff and coordinate CBRN defense, reconnaissance, and decontamination operations. CBRN Defense Chiefs plan, coordinate and monitor the employment of unit CBRN defense, reconnaissance, and decontamination equipment, and attached capabilities, and serve in the unit combat operations center to perform CBRN warning and reporting, and coordinate CBRN response activities. In addition to advising the Commander on the operational and technical functions associated with CBRN defense, CBRN reconnaissance, CBRN response, and CBRN decontamination, senior-level management Marines (MGySgt to MSgt) also advise the commander and staff on events related to supporting countering weapons of mass destruction (CWMD) in support of combatant command lines of effort and objectives within the supported area of operations. CBRN Defense Chiefs at MSC and higher or joint commands are responsible to assist the CBRN Defense Officer with integrating the execution of CWMD in plans, exercises, and operations through organization, training, and planning. They support operations across the spectrum of special operations as fully integrated special staff members in a variety of special operations forces or joint task organized configurations.
requirements: Must possess PMOS 5711.
Attain promotion to SSgt.

This is required in performance of duties associated with MARFOR to MSC and joint billet(s).

CBRN Defense Specialists MOS 5711 terminates at sergeant. title: Military Police Officer (I)
overview: Military Police Officers perform garrison law enforcement duties at supporting establishments (SE) and operating forces (OPFOR) law enforcement duties within Marine Forces Headquarters and within 4th Law Enforcement Battalion, Marine Forces Reserve. Typical duties and billets at the SE include watch commander, services officer, operations officer, deputy provost marshal, and provost marshal. Typical duties and billets at the OPFOR include platoon commander, company commander, operations officer, executive officer, and commanding officer, and law enforcement integrations officer.

ai.blurb: Leads Marine military police — running base law enforcement operations or commanding MP units in the field.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens on a base, where you might be a watch commander overseeing patrols, an operations officer planning coverage, or eventually the provost marshal running the whole shop. In the operating forces you command a platoon or company of military police instead, handling law enforcement tasks that support deployed Marines. Expect shift work, incident reports, courts and legal paperwork, and a lot of time managing junior Marines who are out on patrol at odd hours.

title: Corrections Officer (III)
overview: Corrections Officers interpret, apply and review policies, regulations and directives; oversee the humane care, custody, discipline, safety, welfare, and correctional treatment of personnel confined at military correctional facilities (MCFs); review and recommend treatment programs, custody classification and other security, control and disposition matters related to the confinement or restraint of personnel. They review and make recommendations on clemency, parole and/or restoration to duty requests and other day-to-day requests from confined and restrained personnel. They investigate disturbances and recommend actions regarding discipline and adjustment; research and prepare correspondence and reports. They direct the operational, administrative and logistical activities of a brig regarding personnel administration, supply, training activities, messing, pay and funds accounts, and discipline. Corrections Officers also direct counseling and rehabilitation programs. Corrections Officers also provide commanders with the mission and immediate oversight of regional detention facilities in theater with subject matter expertise on the safe, humane and efficient care of enemy detainees entrusted to their care. Duties and billets include Administration Officer, Programs Officer, Operations Officer, Marine Corps Absentee Collection Center OIC, Detachments OIC, Revocation Hearing Officer, Brig Officer, Executive Officer, and Commanding Officer.
requirements: Must currently hold PMOS 5831.
Must meet eligibility and appointment criteria as prescribed in MCO 1040.42B, WO and LDO accession programs.
Complete the Warrant Officer Basic Course (WOBC) (M02RMN4).

ai.blurb: Runs a military prison — the staff, the rules, the welfare and discipline of everyone confined inside.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens inside a brig or a detention facility in theatre: reviewing custody classifications, signing off on treatment and rehabilitation programmes, investigating disturbances, and writing recommendations on clemency, parole or return to duty. You're also running the place as a business — staffing, supply, training, messing, pay accounts. Expect a lot of paperwork, a lot of difficult conversations with confined Marines, and responsibility for people who very much do not want to be there.
ai.funFact: A military prison is called a brig, a term borrowed from the old navy practice of locking offenders in a ship's brig — the compartment named after the two-masted vessel.
goodFitIf: You already serve as a 5831 corrections Marine
You stay calm when people don't
You can hold a standard under pressure
Paperwork doesn't frighten you

Criminal Investigation Officers manage and provide subject matter expertise on criminal investigative operations in both supporting establishment and deployed/combat contingency environments. Criminal Investigation Officers also liaise and coordinate with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies on behalf of the Provost Marshal.

ai.blurb: Polices Marine Corps bases — patrols, traffic stops, accident investigations and security for the installation commander.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens on an installation: foot and vehicle patrols, traffic enforcement, responding to calls, writing up accidents and crime reports, and manning gates and security posts. Shifts run around the clock, so nights, weekends and holidays are normal, and you answer to a patrol supervisor or watch commander. ai.blurb: Investigates felonies and misdemeanors inside the Marine Corps, from crime scenes and interviews to courtroom prep.

title: Correction and Detention Specialist
overview: Correctional Specialists guard and provide 24-hour supervision of the daily activities of confined personnel at military correctional facilities (MCFs) to prevent disturbances and escapes. Correctional Specialists perform routine inspections, process personnel for confinement and release, transport prisoners, absentees and deserters; manage prisoner's funds and personal property, observe and report meaningful changes in prisoner behavior, report conduct investigations on infractions of the MCFs published regulations, investigate the whereabouts of military deserters to facilitate their swift return to military control. Corrections Specialist also provide commanders with the capability to execute regional detention facilities in theater with immediate oversight and subject matter expertise on the safe, humane and efficient care of enemy detainees entrusted to their care. Typical duties and billets include escort, dorm supervisor, master control supervisor, mess deck supervisor, duty driver, duty brig supervisor, command investigator, administration chief, programs chief, and operations chief billets.

They assist the commander in coordination and future planning in support of operations and exercises. The Aviation Radar Systems Officer coordinates the execution of current operations and provides garrison support to operations in support of resident and deployed detachments. Non-Fleet Marine Forces billet assignments for the GBAD Maintenance Officer include Training and Maintenance Officer at the Marine Corps Communication-Electronics School and Acquisition Project Officer at Marine Corps Systems Command. The GBAD Maintenance Officer should complete the MACCS Warrant Officer course after selection to Warrant Officer. PMOS is not dependent upon the completion of this course. Upon appointment to warrant officer, PMOS 5930 is assigned.

title: Aircraft Maintenance Engineer Officer (II/III) (LtCol to Capt) and
overview: Aircraft Maintenance Engineer Officers (AMEOs) are responsible for management of aircraft maintenance and aeronautical repair matters. To be effective, AMEOs must possess a detailed, working knowledge of all Navy sponsored aviation maintenance programs and processes governed by reference (af). AMEOs must possess skills in managing resources with emphasis on efficient personnel employment, maintaining equipment readiness, and exercise/deployment planning. A high level of technical expertise is required to manage the execution of tasks within aviation maintenance. A small population of AMEO's are placed throughout Marine Corps aviation, complementing the talents of the MOS 6002 population. Unlike MOS 6002, whose career path and school may lead to command, the 6004 will remain focused on the technical, procedural, planning and managerial details associated with organizational and intermediate level maintenance in support of shore based, sea based, and expeditionary operations. Warrant Officers and Junior Chief Warrant Officers generally serve in flying squadrons while more Senior Chief Warrant Officers generally serve as Division Officers within the Marine Aviation Logistic Squadron (MALS). While the minimum requirements in paragraph (b) serve as a threshold, a range of characteristics indicating management knowledge exists including training and documented management knowledge/skill. Management experience in organizational and intermediate levels both provide solid backgrounds for this restricted officer MOS as the task of an AMEO is to plan and solve complex management problems and not to have specific knowledge of repairing any one equipment or aircraft type. Applicants with both organizational and intermediate level maintenance experience are considered ideal candidates for appointments to MOS 6004 Limited Duty Officer (LDO). MOS 6004 shall not be assigned as a secondary MOS.

title: Aviation Maintenance Data Specialist
overview: Aviation Maintenance Data Specialists maintain electronic aeronautical records within a computerized maintenance management system. They receive, compile, and record aeronautical component information from maintenance work orders and aircraft diagnostic systems to provide up to date information for maintenance scheduling. This includes the receipt and/or transfer of aircraft, engines, and tracked repairable components. Screening includes updating change management, engineering change proposals, and modifications for applicability to assigned aeronautical equipment. Responsibilities include tracking of naval aircraft flight record flight information and smart aircraft portable memory devices to maintain up to date usage for applicable equipment. In addition, Aviation Maintenance Data Specialist will initiate, maintain, close out, and reinitiate aeronautical component records. They maintain records on components that have service life limits and will monitor accumulations of forced removal items per engineering usage standards. Aviation Maintenance Data Specialist are required to prepare maintenance data reports and correspondence within aircraft maintenance and repair activities. They are also responsible for trend interpretation/analysis in support of aviation readiness reporting requirements to aid maintenance leadership and logisticians in the performance of aviation maintenance related tasks.

title: Avionics Officer (II/III) (LtCol to Capt) and
overview: Avionics Officers (AVOs) direct the Avionics division/ department efforts in order to provide leadership, coordination, and technical subject matter expertise in support of the organizational/ intermediate level mission. Cognizant areas of oversight include aircraft maintenance, avionics systems and component maintenance, avionics support equipment maintenance, integrated logistics resource management, and technical professional development. AVOs are the subject matter experts on all avionics related matters and serve as the staff advisor to the commanding officer and other staff officers throughout the organization. The AVO is directly responsible to the commanding officer for the management, administration, and control of the Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), Aircraft Survivability Equipment (ASE), on-aircraft Digital Interoperability (DI) systems and the (Local Element) Key Management Infrastructure (KMI) System program. Warrant Officers and junior Chief Warrant Officers (CWO2/3) generally serve in operational flying squadrons while more senior Chief Warrant Officers (CWO4/5) generally serve as Assistant AVOs within the Marine Aviation Logistic Squadron (MALS) or AVOs at training commands. Additionally, unique billets (i.e. Fleet Introduction Team, HMX-1, VMX-1) will expose AVOs to program management, acquisitions, and manpower production/management experiences. Management experience in both the organizational and intermediate levels provide solid backgrounds for the restricted officer 6302 MOS as the task of an AVO is to plan and solve complex management problems and not to have specific knowledge of repairing any one equipment or aircraft type. Applicants with a wide breadth of aircraft platforms and avionics systems, program management, and acquisitions expertise are considered ideal candidates for appointments to MOS 6302 limited duty officer (LDO). MOS 6302 shall not be assigned as an secondary MOS.
requirements: Security Requirement: secret security clearance eligibility.

Any of these designations are indicators of a Marines technical expertise within an assigned MOS. Applicants may also be considered if they possess an additional designation as a production controller or maintenance controller (AMOS 6011/6012).

Limited Duty Officers (II): (a) Only 6302 chief warrant officers shall apply for appointment as 6302 LDOs. (b) Applicants for MOS 6302 LDO must have demonstrated superior avionics expertise through the exemplary performance of duties as a 6302 chief warrant officer. A successful tour in a flying squadron is a primary indicator for future success as a 6302 LDO.

Warrant Officers (III): (a) Newly promoted 6302 warrant officers must complete The Basic School Warrant Officer Basic Course (WOBC) (M02RMN4), Quantico, VA. (b) Warrant Officers must complete the first available Avionics Officer/Avionics Chief Foundation Course (N2362X2) at NAS Pensacola, FL. (c) Specific assigned billets, coded with an additional skill designator (ASD), must attain the appropriate type and level certification through the Defense Acquisition University (DAU) within 24 months (see MOS 8060). extra.Duties: (1) Responsible to the commanding officer for the operation of the avionics division/department, to include operational, technical, and administrative functions, asset utilization, and configuration management of all squadron avionics assets. (2) Advise the maintenance officer on all avionics division/ department matters pertaining to the ability to support squadron maintenance efforts, training requirements, personnel qualifications, calibration requirements, and current and planned projects within the avionics division/ department. (3) Directs and monitors all avionics logistical transactions, negotiating avionics maintenance evolutions based on supply availability and aviation maintenance demands while evaluating the effectiveness of avionics to respond to published flying hour programs. (4) Ensures all avionics personnel are trained, certified, and capable of safely repairing aircraft, aeronautical components, and aviation support equipment within the scope of their MOS in accordance with applicable instructions. (5) Responsible for the proper handling, updating, managing, auditing, and safeguarding of classified avionics aircraft publications and equipment. (6) Manage and maintains mission essential kits that effect communication, navigation, instrumentation (CNI) mission systems, on-aircraft digital interoperability (DI) mission systems, aircraft survivability equipment (ASE), targeting systems, and fire control systems including all controlled cryptographic item (CCI) and related COMSEC management to ensure assigned squadrons have required capabilities as directed by higher.

ai.blurb: Runs the avionics shop in a Marine aviation squadron, managing the Marines, parts and paperwork that keep aircraft electronics working.
ai.dayToDay: You work out of a squadron or Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron hangar, splitting time between the maintenance floor and a desk full of logistics, training records and classified publications. Your job is less about soldering a circuit card yourself and more about deciding which jobs get done, whether your Marines are certified to do them, and what to tell the commanding officer when parts don't arrive. Expect long maintenance days before flight schedules, deployments afloat or ashore, and a steady stream of audits on cryptographic and survivability gear.
ai.funFact: This isn't an entry-level route: 6302 is a warrant officer and limited duty officer MOS, so you get here by first serving years as an enlisted avionics Marine and proving it on the flight line.
goodFitIf: you like fixing systems, not just boxes
you can hold people to standards
paperwork and audits don't frighten you
you've already worked on aircraft

ai.blurb: Kept the radios, navigation and radar gear working on the Marine Corps' EA-6B Prowler jamming aircraft — a job that no longer exists.
ai.dayToDay: This was squadron-level ("organizational") avionics work: troubleshooting and swapping boxes on the flight line and in the hangar, often at night or in bad weather, so the jets made the next day's schedule. Technicians worked in small maintenance shops alongside plane captains and other avionics specialists, with plenty of wiring diagrams, test benches and paperwork. The MOS has been retired from the Marine Corps table of organization, so nobody is trained into it today — the modern equivalent is avionics work on other airframes.
ai.funFact: The EA-6B Prowler was the Marine Corps' electronic-attack aircraft, built to jam enemy radar and communications; the last Marine Prowler squadron stood down in 2019, taking jobs like this one with it.
goodFitIf: like fault-finding in complex electronics
are patient with wiring and manuals
don't mind night shifts on a flight line
can hold a secret clearance

ai.blurb: Keeps the electronics on Marine Corps drones working — testing, fixing and swapping out avionics gear, then helping launch and recover the aircraft.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens on a flight line or in a maintenance hangar, on the MQ-9A Reaper and its ground equipment. You'll pull and replace boxes, run test sets, trace faults, sign off paperwork, and then stand out on the line for launch and recovery. It's team work with other avionics and airframes Marines, often on shifts, and the pace follows the flight schedule rather than the clock.
ai.funFact: The MQ-9 Reaper is unusual in Marine aviation: nobody sits in it, but the maintenance culture, flight-line procedures and paperwork are much the same as for a manned aircraft.

ai.blurb: Keeps the radios, navigation gear and electronic countermeasures working on the Marine Corps' KC-130 transport and refuelling aircraft.
ai.dayToDay: You work on the flight line and in hangars, often on a squadron's maintenance schedule rather than a nine-to-five, troubleshooting black boxes, wiring and antennas on KC-130s with test equipment and technical manuals. Much of it is inspection and fault-finding — tracing why a radio or navigation system isn't behaving — alongside a small crew of avionics Marines and the airframe and powerplant shops. ai.funFact: The KC-130 is the Marine Corps' flying petrol station and cargo hauler, and its armed variant, the KC-130J Harvest HAWK, can also carry missiles — so the aircraft you maintain does rather more than ferry supplies.

ai.dayToDay: You work in a squadron on the flight line or a carrier deck, pulling and testing black boxes, chasing faults with test sets and wiring diagrams, and signing off that a jet's radar, radios and countermeasures actually work before it launches. You're part of a maintenance crew, working alongside airframers, mechanics and the aircrew who'll fly what you just fixed.
ai.funFact: The F/A-18's defensive electronic countermeasures gear — the kit that confuses enemy radar — falls under this job, which is part of why a secret clearance is required.

ai.blurb: Keeps the radios, navigation, electrical and countermeasures systems working on the Marine Corps' heavy-lift CH-53 helicopters.
ai.dayToDay: You work at squadron level on the flight line and in the hangar, which means fixing aircraft that are flying today rather than stripping them down in a depot. A shift might involve troubleshooting a faulty comms box with a wiring diagram and a multimeter, running system tests before launch, or spending hours tracing an intermittent fault through a harness. Expect noise, weather, night shifts, deployments afloat and ashore, and a small shop of avionics Marines who know each other's work very well.
ai.funFact: The CH-53 is the Marine Corps' heavy-lift helicopter — the older Super Stallion earned the nickname "Hurricane Maker" for the downwash from its seven rotor blades, and the newer CH-53K King Stallion is far more digital, so avionics work has grown accordingly.
goodFitIf: enjoy methodical electrical fault-finding
can keep calm under flight-line pressure
like aircraft but prefer fixing them
are precise about paperwork and procedure

ai.dayToDay: This MOS is obsolete and no longer appears in the Marine Corps table of organization, so nobody enlists into it today. When it existed, the work happened on squadron flight lines and in hangars: tracing wiring faults, testing generators and instruments, and signing off electrical systems on the EA-6B before it flew. Training ran through the Aviation Electricians Mate course at NAS Pensacola, then an EA-6B-specific course at NAS Whidbey Island, Washington.
ai.funFact: The EA-6B Prowler was the electronic-warfare jet the Marines and Navy used for decades to jam enemy radar; the Marine Corps retired its last Prowlers in 2019, which is why jobs like this one disappeared with the airframe.

title: Avionics Chief
overview: Avionics Chiefs (AVCs) serve as senior enlisted leaders and subject matter experts on all avionics related matters. They provide critical support to the Avionics Officer, Aircraft Maintenance Officer, and at times the Commanding Officer in directing Avionics division/department efforts, ensuring effective leadership, coordination, and technical expertise in support of organizational and intermediate-level mission objectives. They supervise the maintenance and repair of aircraft avionics systems, equipment, and components at the Organizational Maintenance Activity (O-Level) and Intermediate Maintenance Activity (I-Level) levels. Additionally, the Avionics Chief also serves as the alternate for the management, administration, and control of critical systems, including Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), Aircraft Survivability Equipment (ASE), on-aircraft Digital Interoperability (DI) systems, and serves as the squadrons Tier III, Local Element Key Management Infrastructure (KMI) System program. Master Sergeants typically serve as Avionics Chiefs (AVCs) in the operational flying squadrons and Assistant Avionics Chief (A/AVC) at the Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron (MALS). At the I-Level, the Avionics Chief serves as the 63XX/64XX OccFld representative for all MOS's within the MAG. Unique billets (i.e. Fleet Introduction Team, HMX-1, VMX-1, & MMEA) provide experience in program management, acquisition, and manpower production/management experiences. This diverse experience prepares AVCs for complex management challenges and high-visibility billets (HVB's) at MARFOR, Wing, HQMC, and select naval/joint assignments.
